title: Parts Work — Internal Double Crux
metadata_mapping: Canonical frontmatter follows the existing strict entity schema. Richer recommendation metadata stays in this sidecar; the current search index does not automatically ingest these queries.

patterns.title: Internal Double Crux
patterns.domain: Parts work, self-reflection, and applied rationality
patterns.short_description: Let conflicting inner perspectives exchange what each is missing, without deciding the winner in advance.
use_when: A recurring should conflicts with an actual preference or behavior.
Two understandable concerns keep overriding one another.
A plan seems reasonable but a reservation has not received a fair hearing.
goals: Identify assumptions, omissions, and practical constraints
Permit a decision or an unresolved ending without forcing agreement
mechanisms: Represent each perspective with a fair name and first-person contributions
Alternate substantive acknowledgment with one concern at a time
Notice bias in the moderator stance
Check the interpretation against experience and external constraints
prerequisites: A manageable disagreement and enough room to consider both perspectives
Willingness to record uncertainty without making it verbally persuasive
not_ideal_when: The aim is to make an inconvenient concern surrender to a predetermined plan.
An immediate practical need or genuine resource constraint is being displaced by repeated inner negotiation.
example_user_queries: Part of me wants to do this and another part keeps pulling back.
I know what I should do but I keep resisting it.
How can I understand both sides of an argument inside my head?
I want to keep my promise but I also need a boundary.
Every time I commit to something I start wanting to escape it.
My reasons sound convincing but something still feels wrong.
I keep switching between pushing myself and giving up.
I want to hear my hesitation without automatically obeying it.
Can I make a decision without pretending all of me agrees?
I can explain one side clearly but the other is just a feeling.
I am worried I am talking myself into something I do not want.
How do I tell whether this conflict needs more understanding or a real tradeoff?

practice.format: Offline guided writing with up to three exchanges, participant-controlled loop stopping, and a closing reflection
practice.boundary: Educational adaptation: optional acknowledgments and questions, a bounded exchange, and explicit permission to leave disagreement unresolved. The participant writes both perspectives; no AI interpretation, diagnosis, agreement score, or automatic decision is used.

visual.reason: The worked dialogue makes acknowledgment and concern visible directly. A convergence diagram could imply that agreement is the required outcome.

sources.title: CFAR / Duncan Sabien, Internal Double Crux
sources.supports: The named technique, charitable naming, embodied perspectives, alternating acknowledgment and one concern, and a moderator stance. The author labels the technique preliminary and without formal research backing.

sources.title: Anna Salamon, Comment reply: my low-quality thoughts on why CFAR didn't get farther with a real/efficacious art of rationality
sources.supports: First-person retrospective concerns that verbal reasoning and persuasive incentives can overpower less verbal reservations; explicitly framed as personal guesswork.

sources.title: International Focusing Institute, Felt Sense
sources.supports: The distinction between already articulated thoughts or familiar feelings and a less explicitly formulated sense of a situation.

sources.title: Richard Schwartz / IFS Institute, Polarizations Need Your Loving Presence
sources.supports: Comparison with a neighboring IFS model of opposing protective parts and mediation, without equating the approaches.

patterns.evidence_boundary: A preliminary CFAR technique with anecdotal support and substantive retrospective criticism, not a clinically validated self-guided intervention. Examples are fictional. Genuine tradeoffs can remain after the perspectives are understood; felt resolution is not verification of a practical plan.
